items.title: Connected sums of compact connected surfaces, with disk and gluing choices retained
items.statement: Given nonempty compact connected boundaryless surfaces S and T, choose closed embedded disks D_S and D_T lying in coordinate charts and a boundary homeomorphism phi from partial D_S to partial D_T. The connected-sum model S #_phi T is the quotient of (S minus the interior of D_S) disjoint union (T minus the interior of D_T) that identifies each x in partial D_S with phi(x). For oriented surfaces, phi reverses the induced boundary orientations; for unoriented surfaces, phi is part of the model data. Iterated sums retain their disk and gluing data. This definition asserts no independence of those choices. The standard orientable and crosscap models below use the polygon words [a_1,b_1]... [a_g,b_g] and a_1a_1...a_ka_k, respectively.
items.strategy: Give a choice-explicit quotient definition only. Do not claim choice-independence or use connected-sum invariance. Explain that later normal forms use the displayed polygon words as their fixed gluing models.

references.title: Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
Koch, Classification of Surfaces

items.title: The Klein bottle as a square quotient
items.statement: The Klein bottle K is the quotient of the unit square [0,1]^2 by (x,0)~(x,1) and (0,y)~(1,1-y), with the quotient topology. This edge pairing has one face, two edge classes, one vertex class, and one cyclic vertex link, so its realization is a nonempty compact connected boundaryless surface. With counterclockwise boundary traversal its one-polygon word is a b a^{-1} b.
items.strategy: Define the Klein bottle by the explicit square quotient. Check the four-corner equivalence class, the two edge classes, the single cyclic vertex link, the 0/1/2-cell counts, compactness, connectedness, Hausdorffness and second countability. The edge maps and finite separation argument use no full AC. Record the boundary word from the side maps; leave nonorientability and the Euler count to the later example.

items.title: Polygonal schemas and paired boundary edges
items.statement: A polygonal schema is a finite nonempty family of oriented nondegenerate closed disks (polygons or permitted bigons and monogons) whose boundary sides are paired by specified corner-preserving homeomorphisms, affine when both sides are straight; its realization is the quotient by those pairings. It is a connected surface schema when each edge has exactly two incident face-sides and every vertex class has one cyclic link. A one-polygon schema is a connected surface schema with one face; its cyclic boundary word records every paired edge label twice, with the exponent specifying whether boundary traversal agrees with a chosen direction on that edge. Relabelling leaves the quotient unchanged; cyclic rotation and reversal of the word give a homeomorphic quotient. All surfaces on this page are nonempty compact connected boundaryless topological 2-manifolds, with Hausdorff and second-countable topology.
items.strategy: Define the finite polygonal quotient and prove its surface and cell-count properties. The finite union X of closed polygonal disks is compact metric and second-countable; the relation is a finite union of closed edge-pair graphs, diagonal pieces and vertex pairs. Prove q closed by compact projection of R intersect (F times X), then separate distinct compact classes using the published compact-Hausdorff separation theorem. A countable basis of finite unions of rational-rectangle basis elements descends through the closed quotient map. Interior, paired-edge and cyclic vertex-link neighborhoods are disks. The quotient has V vertices, E paired edges and F faces as a finite CW structure. In the one-polygon word, opposite signs are the orientation-compatible pairing and equal signs are twisted; distinguish homeomorphic descriptions from equality of quotient presentations. Empty and boundary cases are excluded; no full AC is used.

references.title: Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
Koch, Classification of Surfaces

items.title: Arc complements and accessible Jordan boundary points
items.statement: If P is the image of an embedding [0,1] into R^2, then R^2\P is polygonally path connected. If C is a Jordan curve and U is a component of R^2\C, points of the plane boundary of U accessible from U by a simple arc whose interior lies in U form a dense subset of that boundary. No choice axiom is assumed. When Jordan separation identifies the boundary with C, this gives a dense accessible subset of C.
items.strategy: For the arc claim derive a finite uniform subdivision from compactness rather than importing a uniform-continuity result. Choose coarse subarcs of diameter <d; use finite subcovers of formula-defined ball families to prove nonadjacent compact subarcs have positive separation without a choice function. Refine to a fine partition and place a 4-by-4 vertex square-grid block at every node. Consecutive blocks overlap in a connected subgrid; groups for adjacent coarse arcs share the endpoint block; nonadjacent groups are disjoint. The union is a finite 2-connected graph; each group or adjacent pair lies in a ball of radius <3d around a point of P, and the arc lies inside its block perimeters. For a bounded face, a generic ray from p to infinity crosses its facial boundary walk oddly, counting any same-face edge twice. Prove by induction on groups that every finite even-degree edge set is a mod-two sum of sets supported in one group or two adjacent groups; decompose them into simple cycles. The face walk has odd parity, while each local cycle has even parity because its support lies in a ball missing p and an outward ray misses that ball. Thus p and q lie in the unique unbounded component, which is polygonally connected and misses P. For accessibility density, stop the segment from an interior point y near a frontier point x at its first exit, defined by a supremum; components of the open complement are open, so the exit lies on C. No AC is used. Thomassen Proposition 2.11 and Hales Figure 11 are construction motivation, not proof text. Lemma 2.10 is not invoked; its omitted span-one case follows directly from its adjacent-pair outer-face hypothesis.

items.title: Finite plane graph ear and face facts
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice for the cited Jordan separation theorem. Every finite connected graph has a spanning tree, and every finite 2-connected graph with at least three vertices has an ear decomposition starting with a cycle. For a finite plane graph whose edges are simple polygonal arcs meeting only at common endpoints, every facial boundary of a 2-connected drawing is a simple cycle and every connected drawing satisfies V-E+F=2. A connected simple bipartite polygonal plane graph with V>=3 satisfies E<=2V-4; in particular K_{3,3} has no polygonal plane drawing. The facial-cycle and Euler conclusions also hold for a finite 2-connected plane graph with one Jordan cycle C drawn by arbitrary simple arcs and every other edge drawn as a simple polygonal arc in the bounded component of R^2\C. All finite combinatorial selections are choice-free.
items.strategy: Prove the spanning-tree and abstract ear-decomposition claims by finite graph arguments. For polygonal 2-connected drawings, reproduce Thomassen Lemma 2.8 (printed pp.120-121): start from a polygonal cycle and add polygonal ears; Lemma 2.4 proves that each added crosscut splits exactly one face and leaves cyclic face boundaries. Use the already published connected polygonal Euler theorem, independently cross-checked against Diestel Theorem 4.2.9, for the general connected case. Count all facial boundary-walk edge incidences, including bridge incidences, for the connected simple bipartite bound; every such walk has length at least four when V>=3. For the hybrid Jordan-boundary case use Thomassen Lemmas 2.13-2.14 (printed pp.122-123): a polygonal crosscut of the bounded Jordan region splits it into two Jordan regions, permitting the same finite ear induction. This hybrid result is exactly the pre-Schonflies interface used in Thomassen Theorem 3.1. Do not assert arbitrary-arc graph face facts until after Schonflies. The only AC is inherited from the Jordan-separation input; all graph selections are finite.

references.title: Thomassen, The Jordan–Schönflies Theorem and the Classification of Surfaces
references.locator: Lemmas 2.4, 2.7-2.8 and 2.13-2.14, printed pp.119-123: polygonal and Jordan-boundary/polygonal-interior graph facts before Schonflies

items.title: Jordan–Schönflies extension for plane curves
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For Jordan curves C and C' in R^2, every homeomorphism h:C→C' extends to a homeomorphism H:R^2→R^2 that maps the bounded and unbounded complementary components of C to the corresponding components of C'. In particular each closed bounded Jordan region is a closed 2-disk.
items.strategy: Use Jordan–Brouwer only for the two-region/common-boundary statement, never for disk closure. Reproduce Thomassen Theorem 3.1: select countable dense accessible boundary sets on both curves, pair them in the cyclic order prescribed by h, and inductively add noncrossing polygonal crosscuts on both sides. At stage n refine finite graphs consisting of the original Jordan boundary and polygonal interior edges so matching face and boundary-arc diameters are <2^{-n}. Thomassen Lemma 2.13 gives the polygonal crosscut of a Jordan region; the preceding graph item supplies precisely Lemma 2.14's hybrid Jordan-boundary/polygonal-interior face and Euler result, ruling out incompatible cyclic joins. No arbitrary-arc graph face theorem is used before this item. Extend matching graph maps over the shrinking Jordan faces and use nested faces to define a continuous bijection on the closed bounded regions, with continuous inverse and boundary map h. Apply the analogous construction to unbounded regions after inversion, then glue along C. AC licenses simultaneous countable choices of accessible points and refinements and is also inherited from Jordan–Brouwer.

references.title: Thomassen, The Jordan–Schönflies Theorem and the Classification of Surfaces
Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
references.locator: Appendix E Theorem E.1, printed p.159, statement only

items.title: Extension of facial plane graph isomorphisms
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite plane graph drawn by arbitrary simple arcs meeting only at common endpoints, every face of a 2-connected drawing has a simple cycle boundary, and every connected drawing satisfies V-E+F=2. A connected simple bipartite plane graph with V>=3 satisfies E<=2V-4, so K_{3,3} has no plane drawing. Moreover, let G and G' be finite 2-connected plane graphs and let an isomorphism carry the cyclic order at every vertex consistently, up to one global reversal, and carry a designated face to a designated face. Then the isomorphism extends to a homeomorphism of the plane carrying every corresponding face onto its mate.
items.strategy: After Jordan–Schönflies, prove the arbitrary-arc plane-graph facts originally scaffolded in the earlier graph item. Use the abstract ear decomposition there and Schönflies to identify each current Jordan face with a disk; an arbitrary embedded ear is a disk crosscut, splitting exactly one face and preserving simple cycle boundaries. The ear count gives Euler for 2-connected graphs; extend Euler to every finite graph by Alexander duality and cellular homology after proving finite graph drawings are compact locally contractible. Count facial boundary-walk incidences, including bridges, to obtain the connected bipartite bound and K_{3,3} obstruction. Given an isomorphism together with a face bijection carrying each frontier cycle and the outer face correctly, extend the induced homeomorphism on each Jordan frontier across its corresponding face by Schönflies, and paste the finitely many extensions. The designated outer face fixes a plane rather than merely sphere extension. AC is inherited from Schönflies.

references.title: Thomassen, The Jordan–Schönflies Theorem and the Classification of Surfaces
Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
references.locator: Appendix E Proposition E.2 and Theorem E.2, printed pp.159–160

items.title: Finite triangulation of a compact connected surface
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every nonempty compact connected boundaryless topological 2-manifold is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite 2-dimensional abstract simplicial complex in which every edge lies in exactly two triangles and each vertex link is a cycle.
items.strategy: Choose finitely many nested closed chart quadrangles covering M. In each chart, take only finitely many older boundary components that reach a wider inner collar; the parameter-interval separation proves finiteness despite arbitrary wild outer contacts. Add 0, 1 or 2 polygonal connectors for whole Jordan-circle components to obtain a 2-connected finite graph, then redraw rooted ears while maintaining an ambient face bijection. A grid-cycle winding argument supplies a nested polygonal separator transverse to the redrawn relevant arcs. Repeat to make all chart boundaries pairwise finite and topologically transverse. Each global complement component lies inside one chart disk; augment its local finite arrangement to 2-connectivity and retain only the added arcs in that component, yielding finitely many closed Jordan disk faces. Use Schönflies to form a regular polygonal face gluing, fan from interior hubs, and take the full vertex-edge-triangle incidence poset to obtain a genuine finite abstract simplicial complex. AC is inherited from chart selection and the Jordan/graph suppliers.

references.title: Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
references.locator: Appendix E Lemma E.2, Theorem E.3 and Chapter 6 Proposition 6.1, printed pp.81–83 and 160–163

references.title: Thomassen, The Jordan–Schönflies Theorem and the Classification of Surfaces

items.title: A finite triangulated surface has a one-polygon schema
items.statement: For a nonempty connected boundaryless topological surface supplied with a finite triangulation, there is a one-polygon surface schema with an equivalent realization. This finite combinatorial reduction uses no choice axiom.
items.strategy: Form the finite dual graph of triangles, with an edge for every shared primal edge; connectedness of the surface makes the dual connected, since a path between face interiors can be perturbed off vertices and across finitely many edges. Choose a maximal acyclic subset of its finitely many edges. If that forest were disconnected, an edge across two components could be added without a cycle; thus it is a spanning tree, with no outside graph theorem needed. Start with disjoint copies of the triangles and glue only the sides represented by tree edges; inductively attach a new triangle along exactly one full boundary side, so the partial union remains a closed disk. Its boundary is one finite polygon; identify the remaining boundary sides according to the original triangulation. The resulting quotient is canonically the original surface. Check that every original edge is glued once in the tree or appears as the unique pair of boundary copies, with no lost vertex relation. The finite tree choice is choice-free.

references.title: Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
Koch, Classification of Surfaces

items.title: Homeomorphism-preserving polygonal schema moves
items.statement: For one-polygon surface schemas, edge subdivision, cyclic rotation, reversal, cancellation of an adjacent inverse pair when another paired edge remains (the sole sphere bigon is terminal), and cutting a polygon along an embedded diagonal followed by regluing paired sides preserve the quotient homeomorphism type. The resulting finite cut-and-paste identities move same-direction pairs together as crosscaps, extract interlaced opposite-direction pairs as commutator handles, and replace one handle plus one crosscap by three crosscaps. Each move preserves the surface link condition; no choice axiom is used.
items.strategy: Prove the basic move inside the convex model polygon by taking a straight chord with endpoints at vertices, cutting the disk into two polygonal disks, and identifying the new chord edges inversely; both quotient descriptions coequalize the same finite boundary equivalence relation, so the induced maps are mutually inverse continuous maps between compact Hausdorff surfaces. A temporary labelled diagonal and edge subdivisions turn the two standard same-sign and opposite-sign word manipulations into finite sequences of basic moves (Koch §5 Lemmas 1–2; Gallier P1/P2). Draw and track all endpoints, inverse signs and cyclic words, and verify the local vertex-link cycle after each regluing. For the mixed move, place a square block next to a commutator block, apply the same two cut-and-paste identities, and obtain three square blocks. This lemma supplies explicit allowable operations, not a claim that arbitrary relabelling of letters preserves a surface.

items.title: Polygonal normal forms for compact connected surfaces
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every nonempty compact connected boundaryless topological 2-manifold has a one-polygon presentation of one of the following forms: the sphere digon (denoted by an empty reduced word after inverse-pair cancellation), a handle word product_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1} b_i^{-1} for some g>=1, or a square word product_{j=1}^k c_j c_j for some k>=1. Mixed handle/crosscap words convert to the square-word form. This existence statement does not assert numerical uniqueness; the classification theorem proves uniqueness and identifies orientability.
items.strategy: First apply finite triangulation and the dual-tree one-polygon lemma. Follow Gallier–Xu Lemma 6.1 six-stage algorithm: cancel adjacent inverse edges; reduce vertex classes by an inner move that shortens one selected cyclic class, followed by adjacent inverse cancellation that lowers V and E, then repeat until one vertex class remains; if a same-direction pair exists, cut and reglue to place it as an adjacent square; otherwise find interlaced inverse pairs and extract a commutator; repeat on the remaining finite letters. Measure progress by the number of unprocessed paired letters after the initial finite vertex reductions, so the procedure terminates. If both block types occur, use the proved handle-plus-crosscap-to-three-crosscaps move until only squares remain. Track that every quotient remains a compact surface and its realization is homeomorphic to the initial manifold. AC is used solely through the finite-triangulation supplier.

references.title: Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
Koch, Classification of Surfaces

items.title: Torus commutator polygon
items.statement: The square with boundary word a b a^{-1} b^{-1} realizes S^1×S^1, is orientable, and has V=1,E=2,F=1 and chi=0. This direct finite quotient uses no choice axiom.
items.strategy: Identify opposite square sides by translations. The quotient map [0,1]^2→(R/Z)^2 is continuous, surjective and descends to a continuous bijection from a compact quotient to a Hausdorff torus, hence a homeomorphism. Both translations preserve the local plane orientation; check all four corners form one vertex class, so the cell count is 1-2+1=0.

items.title: Projective plane crosscap polygon
items.statement: The digon with boundary word a a realizes RP^2, is nonorientable, and has V=1,E=1,F=1 and chi=1. This direct finite quotient uses no choice axiom.
items.strategy: Realize RP^2 as the closed northern hemisphere of S^2 with antipodal boundary points identified; map the digon disk to that hemisphere so its two sides pair in the same boundary direction. The induced compact-to-Hausdorff quotient bijection is a homeomorphism. The two digon vertices coalesce; count 1-1+1=1. A loop through the paired edge reverses a local orientation, so an integral orientation section cannot exist.

items.title: Sphere as a polygonal quotient
items.statement: The digon with boundary word a a^{-1} is a surface schema homeomorphic to S^2. It has two vertex classes, one edge and one face, so chi=2, and it is orientable. This finite example uses no choice axiom.
items.strategy: Draw the two directed sides of the digon and glue according to opposite boundary exponents; their two endpoints remain distinct. Use the adjacent-inverse cancellation move to reduce the quotient to the empty word, whose disk boundary is collapsed as the standard sphere model, or exhibit the two hemisphere charts directly. Count V=2,E=1,F=1 and transport an orientation across the inverse pairing.

items.title: Classification of compact connected surfaces
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Every nonempty compact connected boundaryless topological 2-manifold is homeomorphic to S^2, to the connected sum of g tori for a unique g>=1, or to the connected sum of k real projective planes for a unique k>=1. Two such surfaces are homeomorphic if and only if they have the same integral orientability and the same Euler characteristic. The sphere digon has empty reduction notation; the other canonical polygon words are the g-fold commutator word, and the k-fold square word, respectively.
items.strategy: Identify canonical word blocks with sphere, torus and projective-plane connected-sum models by cutting polygonal interior disks, gluing their boundaries, slitting the resulting annulus across the seam, and contracting the bridge edge in a PL disk neighbourhood; these are finite polygon moves, so no connected-sum independence theorem is silently assumed. For an orientable g-handle word, check all edge identifications reverse the boundary traversal and hence glue the face orientation; for a square word, follow a loop through one same-direction pairing to obtain orientation-reversing monodromy. The published local orientation definition and top-homology theorem confirm that orientability is invariant under homeomorphism (over Z, H_2 is Z versus 0). Count one face, 2g edges and one vertex in the g-word to get chi=2-2g; count one face, k edges and one vertex in the k-word to get chi=2-k; the sphere has chi=2. Euler–Poincare plus functoriality of singular homology makes chi a homeomorphism invariant. Within each orientability family these integer formulas are injective; opposite families cannot be homeomorphic by orientation. Conversely matching invariants select the same canonical model from normal form. AC is inherited from the finite-triangulation supplier; Euler and orientation computations themselves need no new choice.

items.title: Euler characteristic of an orientable compact surface
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A nonempty compact connected orientable boundaryless topological 2-manifold has a unique genus g>=0 (g=0 for the sphere) and Euler characteristic 2-2g. In particular its Euler characteristic is even and at most 2.
items.strategy: Use the orientable branch of classification. For g=0 take the sphere count 2; for g>=1 count the 1-face, 2g-edge, 1-vertex canonical polygon. The theorem makes the count independent of triangulation and g unique. Solve g=(2-chi)/2 and check the nonnegative integer domain. AC is inherited from classification.

Koch, Classification of Surfaces

items.title: Orientability and Euler characteristic determine a nonempty compact connected boundaryless surface
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. For nonempty compact connected boundaryless topological 2-manifolds M and N, M is homeomorphic to N if and only if they have the same integral orientability and chi(M)=chi(N). Euler characteristic alone is not asserted to classify them.
items.strategy: In the forward direction carry orientation sections through the homeomorphism and transport singular homology, then use Euler–Poincare as in the classification theorem. In the reverse direction classify each surface. Matching orientation chooses the same family and matching chi gives the same integer g or k by 2-2g or 2-k, hence the same canonical polygon quotient. AC is inherited from classification.

references.title: Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
Koch, Classification of Surfaces

title: Classification of Compact Connected Surfaces: Examples

items.title: Klein bottle as two crosscaps
items.statement: The one-polygon word a a b b realizes the Klein bottle, equivalently the standard square word a b a^{-1} b under polygonal cut-and-paste. It is nonorientable, has V=1,E=2,F=1 and chi=0. No choice axiom is used.
items.strategy: Cut the standard Klein rectangle along a diagonal, regroup the two resulting crosscap digons, and apply the verified word moves to obtain aabb; conversely reglue to recover the rectangle model. Check the vertex equivalence from the four boundary corners and the one-face count. Either same-direction edge identifies local orientations with opposite signs, giving nonorientability. The two a/a and b/b square blocks are precisely two projective-plane crosscaps.

references.title: Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
Koch, Classification of Surfaces

items.title: Genus-two orientable polygon
items.statement: The octagon word a b a^{-1} b^{-1} c d c^{-1} d^{-1} realizes the connected sum of two tori. It is orientable and has V=1,E=4,F=1 and chi=-2. No choice axiom is used.
items.strategy: Split the octagon along a separating circle that cuts between the two commutator blocks, obtaining two punctured torus square models; join their circular boundaries to identify the connected sum. Check all paired edges reverse boundary direction, so the face orientation glues. Trace vertex identifications to one class and count 1-4+1=-2.

references.title: Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
Koch, Classification of Surfaces

items.title: Equal Euler characteristic without homeomorphism
items.statement: The torus and Klein bottle are nonempty compact connected boundaryless surfaces with equal Euler characteristic 0 but are not homeomorphic: the torus is orientable and the Klein bottle is nonorientable. Thus Euler characteristic alone does not classify such surfaces. No choice axiom is used.
items.strategy: Use the two explicit finite polygon computations, both with V=1,E=2,F=1. Pullback of any integral orientation section along a homeomorphism would give a section on the other surface. The torus has a compatible section and the Klein same-direction edge reverses it, a contradiction. This uses only the examples and the definition of orientation, never the AC-dependent classification theorem.

references.title: Gallier and Xu, A Guide to the Classification Theorem for Compact Surfaces
Koch, Classification of Surfaces
